stem: A product manager says the new upload-and-summarize flow for PDFs "must be seamless and reliable." The developer has to turn this into something the team can build and mark pass or fail. Which statement is a testable functional requirement?

options.text: For PDFs up to 50 pages, return a summary naming every section heading, or a clear error, within 20 seconds.
options.why: Names an input range, an observable output, an error behaviour, and a time bound, so each run can be marked pass or fail.

options.text: Stream the summary from the most capable model with prompt caching so the flow feels seamless.
options.why: This is a mechanism (model, streaming, caching), not a requirement; it presumes a design before the behaviour is defined.

options.text: Support tickets about the summarizer should stay low after launch, reviewed each quarter.
options.why: A lagging business indicator measured quarterly; it cannot gate a build or a release and says nothing about any single run.

options.text: Summaries must be high quality, feel seamless, and come back fast enough that users never notice any waiting at all.
options.why: Restates the goal with more adjectives; no observation would prove it broken, so it cannot be tested.

explanation: Vague goals such as seamless, reliable or accurate must be converted into behaviours someone can observe and mark pass or fail: bounded inputs, a concrete output, defined error handling, and a measurable limit. Mechanisms and lagging indicators are not requirements.
reference: Claude Code docs — Best practices for Claude Code (give Claude verifiable success criteria)

stem: A ticket asks a developer to put a response cache in front of a Claude-backed policy-lookup service because repeated questions are slow and costly. Reading the system, the developer notices the service is shared by several tenants, every answer is written to an audit log, and invalidation on policy updates differs by code path. None of this is mentioned in the ticket. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Set a p95 latency target for lookups and choose a cache TTL that meets it.
options.why: A performance target says nothing about which tenant may see which answer or what the audit log must contain; correctness cannot be inferred from it.

options.text: Elicit the tenancy, invalidation and audit invariants as requirements before designing the cache.
options.why: These standing constraints predate the ticket and decide the design (per-tenant keys, what counts as an auditable answer, when entries expire); they must be established, not discovered by failure.

options.text: Copy the cache design of the neighbouring search service, which already runs reliably in production.
options.why: Reuse imports the other system's assumptions; the search service may be single-tenant or unaudited, so similarity of shape proves nothing.

options.text: Prototype the cache behind a feature flag, ship it to a few tenants, and refine the invalidation rules from production feedback.
options.why: Iteration needs a signal; a tenant served another tenant's answer is silent, rare and expensive, so production feedback arrives as an incident.

explanation: Requests describe the change; the system holds the constraints. Multi-tenancy, an audit obligation and path-dependent invalidation are standing constraints that must be elicited before a design is chosen, because a violation is silent and expensive rather than loud and cheap.
reference: Anthropic engineering — Building effective agents

stem: The functional behaviour of a claims-triage assistant is fully specified. The team must now decide between calling the Claude API directly or using a cloud platform such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry. Which pieces of information should they obtain before deciding? (Choose three.)

options.text: Peak request and token volume, so limits and capacity can be planned.
options.why: Volume at peak is an infrastructure requirement that decides whether a platform's limits and throughput options fit.

options.text: Where inference and stored data must run under the applicable regulation.
options.why: Residency and retention rules filter the candidate list; they are not weighed against cost or latency.

options.text: Which identity provider and credentials must act, and what audit trail is required.
options.why: Identity and audit obligations decide whether billing and IAM must run through an existing cloud account and how requests are attributed.

options.text: Which platform the team used on its most recent project.
options.why: Familiarity orders the options that survive the constraints; it never produces the list.

options.text: The final wording of the system prompt, since each platform interprets prompts differently.
options.why: The same model behaves the same on each platform; prompt wording does not decide the deployment.

options.text: The team's preferred programming language, since each platform requires its own SDK.
options.why: The official SDKs reach the Claude API and the cloud platforms from the same languages, so language does not decide the deployment.

explanation: Once behaviour is specified, a platform decision is made from infrastructure requirements obtained by asking: latency and volume, processing and storage location under a named regulation, and identity, billing and audit obligations. Familiarity and prompt details do not decide it.
reference: Claude API docs — Data residency; Claude API docs — Rate limits

stem: An order-support assistant has a 99.9% availability target for the customer-facing experience. Claude API incidents and 529 overload responses are outside the team's control. Which requirements should the developer add to the solution design so the target can be met? (Choose two.)

options.text: A defined degraded mode, such as queued replies or a non-AI fallback, that keeps the experience available when the model is unreachable.
options.why: Availability is designed at the user-facing boundary; a specified fallback keeps the product available during a dependency outage.

options.text: Request timeouts and bounded retries with backoff, with availability measured at the user rather than at the API.
options.why: Timeouts and bounded retries stop a slow dependency from consuming the whole error budget, and the target must be measured where the requirement was stated.

options.text: A higher max_tokens value so that fewer requests fail.
options.why: max_tokens affects truncation, not availability; a 529 or an outage fails the request regardless.

options.text: Confirmation from Anthropic that the API's own uptime meets 99.9%, so the target is inherited.
options.why: A dependency's uptime does not transfer to the product; the team's own timeouts, retries and fallback decide the user-facing number.

options.text: Retrying every failed call until it succeeds so that no request is ever lost.
options.why: Unbounded retries hold users waiting indefinitely and amplify load during an overload; they lower availability as experienced by the user.

options.text: Sending each request to two model tiers at once and using whichever answers first.
options.why: Doubles cost on every request and does nothing during an API-wide outage that affects both tiers.

explanation: An availability target on a product that depends on an external model API is met by design: a defined degraded mode, timeouts, bounded backoff retries, and measurement at the user. Inheriting the provider's uptime, retrying forever or duplicating requests do not satisfy it.
reference: Claude API docs — Claude API errors; Claude API docs — Rate limits

stem: A read-only FAQ assistant is being extended so it can also issue refunds through the billing API when a customer asks. Which requirements does this change introduce that the read-only version did not need? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each refund execution must be idempotent so a retried request cannot pay the same refund twice.
options.why: A write action with retries needs a key the receiver recognises; reads never had this problem.

options.text: Answers must now be streamed to reduce perceived latency.
options.why: Streaming is a user-experience choice that applies equally to a read-only assistant; it is not created by adding refunds.

options.text: Authorization for a refund must be enforced server-side against the acting customer's identity, and each executed refund recorded for audit.
options.why: Money moves on the model's decision, so who may refund what must be enforced outside the prompt and every action must be attributable.

options.text: The shared system prompt must be cached because refund requests are frequent.
options.why: Caching is a cost optimisation independent of whether the assistant can write; it is not a new requirement.

options.text: The model must be switched to the most capable tier because money is involved.
options.why: Model choice follows evals against the task; the stakes are handled by authorization, idempotency and audit controls, not by tier alone.

options.text: The context window must be enlarged to hold the billing API documentation.
options.why: The billing API is exposed as a tool definition; its documentation is not loaded into context, and window size is unrelated to the write capability.

explanation: Adding a write action changes the requirement set: the action must be safe to repeat, authorized server-side for the acting user, and recorded for audit. Streaming, caching, model tier and context size are unrelated to the new risk.
reference: Anthropic engineering — Building effective agents; MCP specification — Authorization

stem: A US bank must re-score 80,000 transactions every night. The run starts at 01:00, and downstream reporting is hard-blocked until it finishes, which must be by 05:00. Compliance requires that inference run only on US infrastructure, and cost should be as low as possible within those constraints. Which approach satisfies every requirement?

options.text: Call the Messages API synchronously with the default global inference geo, which offers the best availability and therefore the most reliable way to meet the 05:00 deadline.
options.why: Meets the deadline but violates the residency constraint, which filters options rather than trading against them.

options.text: Submit one Message Batch at 01:00 with inference_geo set to "us", since batches cost half as much and most of them finish in well under an hour, leaving ample margin.
options.why: Cheapest, but the only guarantee is a 24-hour window; a batch slowed by demand can miss the 05:00 hard deadline.

options.text: Call the Messages API with bounded concurrency, prompt caching on the shared prefix, and inference_geo "us", keeping batches for deadline-tolerant work.
options.why: Realtime calls give the team control over completion time, caching cuts cost, and the geo setting meets residency; this is the only option that meets the deadline, residency and cost together.

options.text: Split the work into ten smaller Message Batches so each one completes sooner.
options.why: Splitting does not change the guarantee; each batch still has only the 24-hour window, so the hard deadline remains at risk.

explanation: A hard deadline shorter than the Batch API's 24-hour window is a constraint the batch cannot guarantee, however cheap it is, and a residency rule is a filter, not a preference. The realtime API with bounded concurrency, caching and a pinned inference geo is the only option that satisfies deadline, residency and cost at once.
reference: Claude API docs — Batch processing; Claude API docs — Data residency

stem: Finance approves an interactive document-summarization feature only if model spend stays under a fixed monthly ceiling at a forecast volume of about 1.2 million requests, and users wait for each answer. Which requirements make the ceiling enforceable rather than hoped for? (Choose two.)

options.text: A per-request budget for input and output tokens derived from the ceiling and the forecast volume, enforced with max_tokens and bounded context.
options.why: Turns money into a unit the code can enforce on every request; without it no single call is constrained.

options.text: Monitoring of tokens per request and burn rate against the ceiling, with alerts and a decided action when the plan is exceeded.
options.why: A ceiling needs a leading indicator and a pre-agreed response, not a month-end surprise.

options.text: Routing all traffic through the Message Batches API to take the discount on every request.
options.why: Users wait for each answer; the asynchronous 24-hour window does not fit an interactive feature.

options.text: Relying on the organization's monthly spend cap in the Console to stop requests at the ceiling.
options.why: The cap is a hard stop that fails every request for the whole organization; it produces an outage, not a feature that stays within budget.

options.text: Choosing the smallest model tier now so that cost cannot exceed the plan.
options.why: Unit price alone bounds nothing while tokens per request can still grow, and tier should follow evals against the task.

options.text: Enabling prompt caching, since cached tokens are cheaper and the ceiling will then follow.
options.why: Caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix but sets no limit; spend can still grow with uncached input and output.

explanation: A cost ceiling is a business requirement; it becomes enforceable only when translated into a per-request token budget the code applies and a monitored burn rate with a decided response. Discounts, caching and cheaper tiers change the price of unbounded usage, and an organization-wide spend cap is an outage rather than a control.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits (spend limits); Claude API docs — Context windows

stem: An internal assistant reads and updates Jira and Confluence on behalf of employees through MCP servers. Security adds three requirements: every write must be attributable to the employee who asked, the assistant must never have more access than that employee, and the audit trail inside Jira must show the employee rather than a bot. The prototype uses one service account with admin scope. Which design meets all three?

options.text: Have the MCP servers act with each employee's own delegated credentials, so scope and attribution follow the user.
options.why: Per-user delegated authorization means every action carries the employee's identity and permissions into Jira, satisfying attribution, least privilege and the native audit trail.

options.text: Create one service account per team holding the union of that team's permissions.
options.why: Reduces scope but still exceeds any single employee's access, and Jira attributes writes to the team account.

options.text: Instruct the model in the system prompt to check the employee's permissions before writing.
options.why: Prompt instructions are not an enforcement mechanism; the credentials still hold admin scope and attribution is unchanged.

options.text: Keep the single service account but record the requesting employee's ID beside each action in the application's own audit log, exported to security monthly.
options.why: Jira's own trail still shows the bot, and the assistant keeps admin scope, so two of the three requirements fail.

explanation: Whose credentials act is an infrastructure requirement. When actions must be attributable to and bounded by the requesting user, the integration must act with that user's delegated credentials rather than a shared service account, regardless of what the prompt says or what the application logs separately.
reference: MCP specification — Authorization

stem: A Claude-based invoice-coding feature has just gone live after a successful launch review. The project manager wants to close the project and reassign the whole team next week. What must be planned for the feature from this point on?

options.text: A retrospective and a handover document covering architecture, prompts and runbooks, after which no further engineering effort should be expected.
options.why: Both are finite activities; a live system still needs watching and changing after they are done.

options.text: An open-ended operate-and-maintain phase: watching cost, latency, quality and failures, and planning for model retirements and input drift.
options.why: Go-live opens a phase with no completion date; the model can be retired on the provider's schedule and inputs drift, so ownership and monitoring must continue.

options.text: Transfer of the code and its on-call rotation to the platform team, which settles the question of ongoing responsibility for the feature.
options.why: Reassigning ownership answers who does the work; it does not remove the work or define what it is.

options.text: A one-time load test to confirm the deployment can handle peak traffic.
options.why: A useful pre-launch check, but a single activity cannot stand in for the ongoing operate phase.

explanation: In the systems life cycle, deployment is followed by an operate-and-maintain phase that lasts as long as the system does. For a Claude-backed feature that means monitoring, incident response, refreshing evals as inputs drift, and planned migrations when models are deprecated.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations

stem: A support assistant's dashboard shows an HTTP error rate flat at 0.2% and steady p95 latency, yet tickets saying "the bot won't answer" have tripled since the retrieval corpus was changed. Which monitoring gap most likely explains why the dashboard shows nothing?

options.text: Token usage per request is not tracked, so the corpus change went unnoticed.
options.why: Token metrics reveal cost and length changes, not whether the model declined to answer.

options.text: Latency is reported as an average, which hides the slow tail.
options.why: The dashboard already shows p95, and users are complaining about missing answers, not slow ones.

options.text: Refusals return as successful responses with stop_reason "refusal", so an HTTP-error metric never counts them.
options.why: A declined answer is a 200 with a refusal stop reason; a failure count built on transport errors reads flat while usable responses fall, so stop_reason distribution must be tracked.

options.text: The SDK is silently retrying 529 overload errors with backoff, so the failures never reach the error metric even though users see them.
options.why: Retries would raise latency, not produce answered-but-empty replies, and would not correlate with a corpus change.

explanation: Operating a Claude system means counting the failures that arrive as successes. A refusal is delivered on a normal response with stop_reason "refusal", so monitoring must track stop_reason distribution and sampled output quality alongside HTTP errors and latency.
reference: Claude API docs — Stop reasons and fallback

stem: During an incident, on-call discovers that a contract summarizer drops the termination clause for contracts written in French, a case the requirements never mentioned. A prompt tweak fixes it and the incident is closed. What must also happen so the fix survives future releases?

options.text: Pin the model ID so the behaviour cannot change again.
options.why: Pinning holds the model steady, but the defect came from the prompt and the inputs; a later prompt edit could still drop the clause.

options.text: Record the root cause and the prompt tweak in the incident postmortem on the team wiki so future engineers can find it.
options.why: A postmortem preserves knowledge for people; it does not stop the next prompt or model change from reintroducing the defect.

options.text: Raise the canary share from 5% to 20% so similar issues surface sooner.
options.why: A larger canary detects regressions faster in production; it does not prevent this specific regression from shipping again.

options.text: Add French contracts with termination clauses to the requirements and the eval set so every release is gated on them.
options.why: A production finding must flow back into the requirement it contradicts and into the test gate, so the behaviour is checked before each release.

explanation: The iteration step of the life cycle routes production findings back into requirements and the evaluation set, turning a one-off fix into a gated behaviour. Postmortems, larger canaries and model pinning are all sensible but leave the next release free to regress.
reference: Claude API docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A team runs the same Claude model through the Claude API for its web app and through Amazon Bedrock for a regulated workload. Anthropic's model deprecations page now lists a retirement date for that model. Which statements should guide the migration plan? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Bedrock deployment may follow a different retirement schedule, so check that platform's model table rather than assuming the same date.
options.why: Partner-operated platforms set their own retirement schedules, so a model's lifecycle status and dates can differ by where it runs.

options.text: Requests to the model on the Claude API will fail after the retirement date, so the web app must migrate before then.
options.why: Retired models reject requests; the notice period exists so that migration and evaluation complete before the date.

options.text: Bedrock deployments are never affected by Anthropic model retirements.
options.why: Partner platforms retire models too, just on their own published schedules.

options.text: The team can wait for retirement and rely on the API automatically routing requests to the replacement model.
options.why: There is no automatic substitution; requests to a retired model fail.

options.text: Deprecation only means slower responses; the model keeps working indefinitely at lower priority.
options.why: Deprecated means still functional but scheduled for retirement, after which it stops working.

explanation: Model retirement is maintenance driven by the provider's calendar. Anthropic-operated platforms follow the published dates and reject requests after retirement, while partner platforms such as Bedrock and Vertex AI publish their own schedules, so each deployment must be checked and migrated on its own timeline.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations

stem: A team ships one release that changes the model ID, rewrites the system prompt, and swaps the retrieval index. The 10% canary shows a nine-point drop in answer quality against the control. The team wants to recover quickly and avoid a repeat. What is the best approach?

options.text: Roll back the whole release, then reintroduce the three changes one at a time through the eval gate and canary.
options.why: Restores the known-good state immediately and makes each change attributable, which is the only way to find the cause and prevent bundled regressions.

options.text: Widen the canary to 50% to gather more data before deciding.
options.why: Exposes five times as many users to a measured regression; the signal is already clear.

options.text: Keep the release live, since the drop may be noise, and tune the new prompt on the canary until its quality score recovers to the control's level.
options.why: Leaves canary users on a regressed system and cannot tell whether the prompt, the model or the index caused the drop.

options.text: Roll back only the model change, since model upgrades cause most regressions.
options.why: A guess; the drop may come from the index or the prompt, and a partial rollback leaves an untested combination running.

explanation: Change management in the LLM life cycle depends on attribution. Bundling model, prompt and data changes in one release makes a regression impossible to diagnose; roll back to the baseline and promote one variable at a time through evals and a canary.
reference: Claude API docs — Migration guides; Claude API docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem:
An hour after promoting release 42 of an extraction service (prompt v9 to v10, same model, same max_tokens), the on-call engineer sees this comparison:

```
metric                       before   after
http_error_rate              0.3%     0.3%
p95_latency_s                4.1      4.2
stop_reason=end_turn         98%      71%
stop_reason=max_tokens       1%       28%
downstream_parse_failures    0.5%     24%
```

What should the on-call engineer do first?

options.text: Raise max_tokens in production immediately so the outputs stop being truncated, and keep release 42 live while watching the parse failures.
options.why: An untested production change that treats the symptom; the prompt change that made outputs longer has not been evaluated, and cost and latency rise.

options.text: Roll back to release 41 through the versioned runtime config, then reproduce the truncation with prompt v10 offline.
options.why: Restores the last known-good release immediately through versioned configuration, protecting users now, and moves the diagnosis of the prompt change to the eval set instead of production.

options.text: Add a retry when downstream parsing fails.
options.why: Retrying a truncated output produces another truncated output; the parse failures are a consequence, not the fault.

options.text: Open an investigation into the model, since it is generating longer outputs than before.
options.why: The model did not change; the only variable in the release was the prompt, and users are affected now.

explanation: Read the trace: the model and max_tokens are unchanged, the only variable is the prompt, and the max_tokens share rose from 1% to 28% in step with parse failures. The first action is to restore the last good release via versioned configuration, then diagnose prompt v10 offline against the eval set.
reference: Claude API docs — Stop reasons and fallback (max_tokens)

stem: During an outage, one engineer edited a production classifier's prompt directly in the admin panel to stop wrong routings, and a second engineer edited it again. Two days later the eval suite still runs against prompt v7 in git and passes, while production runs an unversioned text nobody can fully reproduce. The current model retires in six weeks. What should the team do first?

options.text: Revert production to v7, since it is the last version that passed the eval suite.
options.why: Reinstates the routing errors the hotfix removed and discards what was learned; v7 passing evals says nothing about the cases the outage exposed.

options.text: Start the model migration now so it finishes comfortably before retirement, folding the two engineers' prompt fixes in along the way.
options.why: Migrating on top of an unmeasured baseline means any change in results cannot be attributed to the model or to the prompt.

options.text: Capture the live prompt as a new version in git, run the eval suite on it, and make it the baseline before migrating.
options.why: Restores measurability first: the running text becomes a tracked, scored version, so the migration six weeks out has a real baseline to compare against.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt from scratch for the replacement model.
options.why: Throws away the fixes and starts the migration with two variables changed at once and no baseline.

explanation: When production and the tracked configuration have diverged, the first step is to restore measurability: version what is actually running, score it, and make it the baseline. Only then can a model migration or any further prompt change be evaluated and attributed.
reference: Claude API docs — Migration guides; Claude API docs — Model deprecations

stem:
A chat assistant's monthly cost has nearly tripled while traffic, model ID, prompt version and output length are unchanged. The usage export shows:

```
month  requests  input_tok/req  output_tok/req  cost_index
Jun    1.02M     3,900          410             100
Jul    1.01M     6,800          420             165
Aug    1.03M     11,500         430             280
```

Which maintenance action addresses the root cause?

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the conversation history so the repeated tokens in every turn are billed at the cheaper cache-read rate.
options.why: Cache reads are cheaper but still grow with the history; it lowers the slope without fixing why input keeps expanding.

options.text: Switch the assistant to a smaller model tier to bring the bill back down.
options.why: Lowers the unit price but leaves input per request growing month over month, so the trend continues.

options.text: Move the assistant's traffic to the Message Batches API for the discount.
options.why: Interactive chat cannot wait on an asynchronous batch, and a discount does not stop the growth.

options.text: Bound the conversation history sent per request by trimming or summarizing older turns, and alert on input tokens per request.
options.why: Input tokens per request are climbing with flat traffic and output, which points to unbounded history accumulating in each request; capping it removes the cause and the alert catches a recurrence.

explanation: Maintenance starts from telemetry. Flat requests and output with input tokens per request tripling means each request carries more context, typically unbounded conversation history. Fix the cause with a history budget and add an alert on the leading indicator; cheaper tiers, batches or caching only change the price of the same growth.
reference: Claude API docs — Context windows; Claude API docs — Prompt caching

stem: A web app lets users request a Claude-generated 60-page report that takes about two minutes to produce. The team is designing the REST endpoint that triggers it. Which design follows REST semantics for a long-running operation?

options.text: POST /reports returns 202 Accepted with a Location header for a job resource the client polls with GET.
options.why: 202 signals that the request was accepted but not completed, and the job resource lets the client poll status and fetch the result when ready.

options.text: POST /reports holds the connection open for two minutes and returns 200 with the finished report in the body.
options.why: Long-held connections hit proxy and client timeouts, and a timed-out client cannot tell whether the report was produced.

options.text: GET /reports?generate=true creates the report, since the client is ultimately reading a result.
options.why: GET must be safe and free of side effects; caches, prefetchers and retries would create reports unexpectedly.

options.text: POST /reports returns 201 Created with an empty body, and the client repeats the POST until content appears.
options.why: Repeating a non-idempotent POST creates a new report job each time and 201 wrongly claims the resource exists.

explanation: Long-running operations in REST use the accepted-then-poll pattern: POST creates a job, returns 202 with a Location for the job resource, and the client polls with GET until it is complete. GET stays side-effect free, and clients never retry a non-idempotent POST to wait.
reference: Claude API docs — Batch processing (asynchronous job pattern)

stem: A job fans out 500 summarization calls with asyncio.as_completed(), appends each result to a list as it arrives, and then writes results[i] back to documents[i]. Some documents end up with another document's summary. What is the cause and the fix?

options.text: Rate limiting reorders responses; add exponential backoff before each call.
options.why: Backoff changes timing, not the fact that completion order differs from submission order.

options.text: as_completed yields in completion order, not submission order; return the document ID with each result and join by ID.
options.why: Completion order is arbitrary under concurrency, so joining by position is wrong; a correlation key carried with each result makes the join correct.

options.text: Sort the results by completion timestamp before writing them back.
options.why: Timestamps encode when calls finished, which is unrelated to which document each call was for.

options.text: The model confuses documents when many calls overlap in flight; run the calls one at a time so each response can only belong to one document.
options.why: Each request is independent; serializing hides the bug by accident and throws away the concurrency.

explanation: In asynchronous code, completion order is not submission order. Every unit of concurrent work should carry a correlation key that comes back with its result (the same idea as custom_id in the Batch API), and results are joined by that key, never by list position.
reference: Claude API docs — Batch processing (custom_id and result ordering)

stem: A pipeline reads support tickets from a durable message queue as fast as they arrive (about 200 per second at peak), places each into an in-memory asyncio.Queue, and 20 workers call Claude at about 40 requests per second in total. During peaks the process's memory grows until it is killed and in-flight tickets are lost. Rate limits rule out adding many more workers. What is the best fix?

options.text: Raise the container's memory limit so the process can buffer a full peak.
options.why: Postpones the crash to a bigger peak and still loses everything in memory when the process dies.

options.text: Increase the worker count to 100 and rely on the SDK's automatic retries with backoff to absorb the resulting 429 rate-limit responses.
options.why: The rate limit is the real ceiling; extra workers only trade memory growth for retry storms and wasted capacity.

options.text: Bound the in-memory queue so the reader blocks (backpressure) and excess tickets wait in the durable queue until a worker is free.
options.why: Bounding the buffer makes the consumer's rate govern the producer, keeps memory constant, and leaves unprocessed tickets safely in the durable queue.

options.text: Drop tickets when the in-memory queue exceeds a threshold and log them for later.
options.why: Load shedding loses work that a durable queue could have held; it converts a memory problem into a data-loss problem.

explanation: Asynchronous pipelines need backpressure: a bounded buffer that blocks the producer when consumers cannot keep up, so throughput is governed by the slowest stage (here the rate-limited Claude calls) and unprocessed work stays where it is durable.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits

stem: A backend exposes POST /summaries, which calls the Messages API. When the upstream call still fails with a 429 or 529 after the SDK's retries, the handler returns HTTP 200 with {"error": "upstream busy"} in the body. Mobile clients treat every 200 as a finished summary and show an empty screen. Which response follows HTTP semantics and lets clients recover?

options.text: Return 503 with a Retry-After header so clients know the failure is temporary and when to try again.
options.why: 503 states that the service is temporarily unable to handle the request, and Retry-After gives clients a backoff they can honor instead of guessing.

options.text: Return 500, since the failure happened on the server side of the request.
options.why: 500 signals an unexpected fault, carries no retry timing, and turns a transient dependency limit into a bug alert.

options.text: Keep 200 and add "status": "failed" to the JSON so clients can check it.
options.why: The status code is the HTTP contract; a 200 that means failure breaks generic clients, caches and monitoring.

options.text: Return 400 so that the client stops resending the request.
options.why: 400 blames the request itself, so clients will not retry a valid request that would succeed a moment later.

explanation: REST APIs communicate outcome through status codes. A transient upstream failure is a 503 (service unavailable) with Retry-After, which tells every client, cache and monitor that the request was valid, nothing was produced, and when to retry. Hiding failure inside a 200 body or reporting it as a 500 or 400 misleads clients.
reference: Claude API docs — Claude API errors

stem: Claude Code opens a pull request adding a summarization endpoint. CI is green. Review finds that the model ID and system prompt are hardcoded in the handler, that a 429 or 529 from the API surfaces as an unhandled 500 to the user, and that the change has no tests. Which review responses are appropriate? (Choose three.)

options.text: Require the model ID and prompt to move into versioned configuration before merge.
options.why: Hardcoded configuration cannot change without a deploy and cannot be rolled back independently; it fails on its own.

options.text: Require handling of transient API errors: backoff honoring retry-after and a defined degraded response for the user.
options.why: Without an error path the first rate limit becomes an outage; rare does not mean harmless.

options.text: Require tests that cover the endpoint's success and error paths.
options.why: Without tests neither the behaviour nor the error handling is verifiable, so the other two fixes cannot be checked.

options.text: Approve now and open a follow-up ticket for the error path, since 529s are rare.
options.why: Defers a gap that fails independently in production; a follow-up ticket does not protect users.

options.text: Approve because CI is green and the code matches the surrounding style.
options.why: A green CI with no tests proves nothing about the change; style is not a merge criterion.

options.text: Fix all three issues yourself in a commit on the PR and merge it.
options.why: Moves the work to the reviewer and merges code nobody else reviewed; the request should go back to the author or the agent session.

explanation: Reviewing AI-written changes uses the same bar as any other: hardcoded configuration, a missing error path and missing tests each fail independently in production, so all three must be addressed before merge. Partial approval or the reviewer patching it privately removes the gate.
reference: Claude Code docs — Best practices for Claude Code (review and verify Claude's work)

stem: Claude Code delivers a single 2,400-line pull request that renames a module, reformats 40 files, fixes a bug in date handling, and adds a new export feature. Reviewers cannot tell which lines matter, and the fix is urgently needed. What should the developer ask for?

options.text: Separate small PRs: the bug fix first, then the rename, the formatting-only change, and the feature, each with tests.
options.why: Small, single-purpose PRs are reviewable, bisectable and revertible, and the urgent fix can land first without waiting on the rest.

options.text: Have Claude Code review its own pull request and post a summary of risks.
options.why: The author session reviewing itself does not restore the human's ability to see what changed.

options.text: Squash-merge the PR so the history stays clean, then revert if problems appear.
options.why: One squashed commit makes the four changes inseparable; a revert would also remove the urgent fix and the feature.

options.text: A detailed PR description explaining each of the four parts, with links to the relevant files, so reviewers can navigate the large diff.
options.why: Helps navigation but leaves reviewers reading behaviour changes buried in formatting noise, and everything still ships or reverts together.

explanation: Version-control hygiene with AI-generated changes means small, single-purpose PRs: behaviour changes separate from refactors and formatting, each with tests. That keeps review meaningful and lets the urgent change ship, bisect and revert independently.
reference: Claude Code docs — Best practices for Claude Code (work in small, verifiable steps)

stem: An SDK parameter the team uses to control model reasoning is deprecated; its replacement acts on a different axis (a discrete effort level instead of a token budget), so behaviour will not map one to one. Twelve call sites across three services are affected and the cutoff is in ten weeks. Which migration plan best manages the risk?

options.text: Write a wrapper that translates the old parameter into the nearest value of the new one so that none of the twelve call sites has to change.
options.why: Keeps the call shape but not the semantics; every site silently behaves differently and nothing was measured.

options.text: Capture each call site's current behaviour with evals, then migrate in small batches, comparing each against baseline.
options.why: Because the replacement changes behaviour, the risk is semantic; pinning behaviour first and migrating in attributable batches keeps every change measurable and revertible.

options.text: Migrate all twelve sites in one PR the week before the cutoff to minimize the time both paths coexist.
options.why: Concentrates every semantic change into one push with no slack left to react if evals or production disagree.

options.text: Remove the parameter now and rely on the model's defaults until the replacement is understood.
options.why: Changes behaviour at all twelve sites immediately without a baseline, which is the same risk with less control.

explanation: When a deprecated parameter's replacement changes behaviour rather than just its name, the risk is semantic, not schedule. Cover current behaviour with tests, migrate in batches small enough to attribute a change to, and leave time before the deadline. Wrappers and deadline-day swaps address only when the work happens.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations (deprecated API parameters); Claude API docs — Migration guides

stem: A team is designing CI for a Claude-backed classification service. The pipeline must fail on real regressions, must not fail when a correct answer is merely reworded, and must never change production without a human decision. Which stages belong in the pipeline? (Choose two.)

options.text: A scored evaluation against a versioned test set with a pass threshold.
options.why: Scores the behaviour that matters, tolerates rewording, and can refuse a change; the artifact it refuses against is versioned.

options.text: Snapshot tests comparing the model's full response text to stored outputs.
options.why: Fires whenever a correct answer is phrased differently, so it reports noise and gets disabled.

options.text: Contract tests that validate the output JSON against the schema downstream parsers expect.
options.why: Catches the regressions that break consumers without caring how the text inside the fields is worded.

options.text: A stage that rewrites the prompt and redeploys automatically when the eval score dips.
options.why: Removes the human decision and deletes the signal the eval was meant to raise.

options.text: A step that merges automatically when the AI code reviewer leaves no comments.
options.why: Treats a reviewer's silence as a gate and changes production without anyone deciding.

explanation: A pipeline stage earns its place if it catches regressions that would otherwise ship and stays green when a correct answer is reworded. Scored evals against a versioned set and schema contract tests meet both; literal snapshots fail the second, and automatic rewriting or merging removes the human decision.
reference: Claude API docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Claude Code docs — Claude Code GitHub Actions

stem: During a traffic spike, a service's logs show the same request ID attempted up to 15 times against the Messages API, all ending in 429. The code wraps each SDK call in its own loop of up to five attempts with a fixed one-second sleep; the SDK client keeps its default retries. Requirements: keep throughput, never amplify a rate-limit event, and avoid duplicate side effects when a call finally succeeds. What should the developer change?

options.text: Catch the 429 and immediately fail the retry over to a second model tier, since each model class has its own separate rate limits.
options.why: Changes which model answers mid-request and leaves both retry loops in place, so the same storm simply moves to the second tier.

options.text: Increase the application loop to ten attempts so more requests eventually get through.
options.why: Multiplies the retry storm (each attempt still triggers the SDK's own retries) and pushes the token bucket further into deficit.

options.text: Keep one retry layer that honors retry-after with exponential backoff, and bound concurrency so retries do not compete with new work.
options.why: Nested retry loops multiply attempts (5 x 3 here); one layer that respects retry-after and a bounded pool stops the amplification while preserving throughput and side-effect safety.

options.text: Disable the SDK's retries and keep the five-attempt application loop with the fixed sleep.
options.why: Removes the multiplication but ignores retry-after; fixed one-second retries keep hitting the limit before it replenishes.

explanation: Retries must live in exactly one layer. Stacking an application loop on top of SDK retries multiplies attempts and turns a rate-limit event into a storm. Use one retry policy that honors retry-after with exponential backoff, keep concurrency bounded, and let idempotent side effects make the eventual success safe.
reference: Claude API docs — Claude API errors (SDK retries); Claude API docs — Rate limits (retry-after)

stem: An extraction service asks Claude for a JSON object containing invoice_id, a 19-digit numeric identifier from the ERP, validated against a schema where invoice_id is an integer. The Node.js consumer reports that about a third of the IDs match no ERP record, and the mismatched ones all end in one or two zeros. What is the root cause and the fix?

options.text: Enable structured outputs so the number the model returns is guaranteed exact.
options.why: Structured outputs guarantee the shape of the JSON, not how a downstream language parses a numeric literal.

options.text: The model rounds long numbers when generating them; add few-shot examples that show exact 19-digit IDs so it reproduces them faithfully.
options.why: The model's text is exact; the loss happens when the consumer parses the number, so prompting cannot fix it.

options.text: Validation is too loose; add minimum and maximum bounds to the integer schema.
options.why: Bounds do not change how the parser represents the number, and 19-digit values are within any sensible range.

options.text: JSON.parse turns numbers into doubles that cannot hold integers above 2^53 exactly; make invoice_id a string in the schema.
options.why: Trailing zeros are the signature of float precision loss on large integers; identifiers should be strings in the schema and never parsed as numbers.

explanation: JSON handling is part of the contract. JavaScript parses JSON numbers into IEEE-754 doubles, so integers above 2^53 lose low-order digits, producing the trailing-zero pattern. Identifiers, account numbers and other non-arithmetic values belong in the schema as strings.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs

stem: A security team wants Claude Code to scan every pull request in CI for hardcoded secrets. Constraints: the job must never modify the repository or wait for input, its findings must be machine-readable so the pipeline can fail the build on any high-severity finding, and it must behave identically on every runner. Which setup best fits?

options.text: `claude --bare -p "<scan prompt>" --allowedTools "Read" --permission-mode dontAsk --output-format json --json-schema <findings schema>`; the pipeline fails on a high finding in structured_output.
options.why: Only reads are pre-approved and dontAsk denies anything else, so the job cannot edit or wait; bare mode removes host-specific configuration; schema-validated JSON lets the pipeline, not the model, decide the build result.

options.text: `claude -p "<scan prompt>" --permission-mode acceptEdits --output-format text`, then grep the printed text for the word HIGH and fail the build whenever that word appears anywhere in the output.
options.why: acceptEdits lets Claude write files, and grepping free text for a word is not a reliable machine-readable contract.

options.text: `claude -p "<scan prompt> and remove any secrets you find" --permission-mode bypassPermissions`, so the job both finds and fixes secrets in one run.
options.why: Violates the no-modification constraint and gives unrestricted permissions to a job that only needs to read.

options.text: The Claude Code GitHub Action in interactive mode, so reviewers read Claude's comment on each PR and decide whether to merge.
options.why: Interactive mode waits for an @claude mention, and a comment for humans is not a gate the pipeline can enforce.

explanation: Headless CI integration maps each constraint to a flag: a read-only --allowedTools entry with dontAsk for no edits and no prompts, --bare for reproducibility, and --output-format json with --json-schema for structured findings. The merge decision is then made by the pipeline reading that output, not by the model.
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically (structured output, permission modes, bare mode)

stem: A monorepo's shared PaymentClient.charge() must be renamed and its signature changed. It has about 1,800 call sites across services that other teams deploy on their own schedules. The platform must stay up throughout, and any regression must be attributable to a small change. How should the team run this refactor with Claude Code?

options.text: Have Claude Code rewrite all 1,800 call sites in one overnight PR, with the full test suite run once at the end, so the codebase is never in a mixed state.
options.why: One giant change cannot be reviewed or attributed, and every service must deploy at once, which their owners cannot do.

options.text: Add the new method beside the old, migrate call sites in small test-gated batches (e.g., claude -p per package), then remove the old method at zero usage.
options.why: Expand, migrate, contract keeps both paths working while teams deploy independently, and each batch is small enough to attribute a failure to.

options.text: Rename the method and keep a permanent wrapper under the old name so nobody has to change call sites.
options.why: The signature change means the wrapper cannot preserve semantics, and the migration never actually happens.

options.text: Rename in place and pin the other teams' builds to the previous commit until they catch up.
options.why: Freezes other teams' deployments and creates a mixed state with no compatible path between versions.

explanation: Large-scale refactors that cross deployment boundaries follow expand-migrate-contract: introduce the new API alongside the old, migrate in small, test-gated batches that Claude Code can fan out per package, and remove the old API only when usage is gone. That keeps the platform up and every change attributable.
reference: Claude Code docs — Common workflows (run large migrations with claude -p)

stem: A project's CLAUDE.md has grown to about 900 lines: it pastes the full style guide, the reference for an internal SDK, and a history of past design decisions. Developers report that Claude now ignores even the basic build and test instructions at the top. What is the best fix?

options.text: Convert the instructions into a PreToolUse hook so they are enforced rather than read.
options.why: Hooks enforce specific actions; they cannot carry a style guide or SDK reference, which are guidance, not blockable events.

options.text: Split the 900 lines into several topic files and @import all of them from CLAUDE.md so each file stays short and easy to maintain.
options.why: Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch, so the context cost and the dilution are unchanged.

options.text: Cut CLAUDE.md to concise essentials and move reference material into path-scoped rules or files Claude reads on demand.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is context, and long files reduce adherence; the guidance is to stay under roughly 200 lines and load detail on demand through path-scoped rules or referenced files.

options.text: Move the content to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it loads consistently for everyone.
options.why: The user file is personal to one machine, and moving the same volume of text does not reduce it.

explanation: CLAUDE.md content hygiene: keep it short, specific and current, because it is loaded as context on every session and long files reduce adherence. Put detail into path-scoped .claude/rules files that load only when matching files are touched, or into documents Claude can open when relevant.
reference: Claude Code docs — How Claude remembers your project (size and organization guidance)

stem: One developer configured a PostToolUse hook in ~/.claude/settings.json that runs the code formatter after every edit Claude makes. The team likes it, and the onboarding runbook now says "copy this hook into your user settings." Some teammates forget, and formatting-only diffs keep appearing in pull requests. What should the team do?

options.text: Put the hook in the repository's .claude/settings.local.json.
options.why: The local file is gitignored and personal, so teammates still would not receive it.

options.text: Deploy the hook through managed settings so that nobody in the organization can skip it, regardless of which repository they work in.
options.why: Managed settings are for organization-wide policy that developers cannot change, not for one team's formatter preference.

options.text: Add a line to CLAUDE.md telling Claude to run the formatter after each edit.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement; the hook exists precisely because a hook runs every time.

options.text: Move the hook into the repository's committed .claude/settings.json so every clone gets it.
options.why: Configuration the whole team depends on belongs in the project file that travels with the repository, reviewed like code.

explanation: Scope follows reach. A setting the team relies on must live in the shared project settings file that is committed with the code; user and local settings reach one machine, and managed settings are reserved for organization policy.
reference: Claude Code docs — Settings files and precedence

stem: A repository's committed .claude/settings.json sets "model" to a specific pinned model so every session behaves the same. One developer keeps starting on a different model. Their shell profile exports ANTHROPIC_MODEL for an unrelated project, and their user settings also set a model. What explains this, and what is the right fix?

options.text: ANTHROPIC_MODEL in the shell applies over the model key from any settings file; unset or scope it rather than editing the shared file.
options.why: The environment variable is decided per pair with the model key and wins over files, so the fix is on the developer's environment, not the repository.

options.text: Project settings are advisory; the pin must be moved into managed settings to take effect.
options.why: Project settings do set the session model; managed settings are for policy the organization enforces, not for a normal team pin.

options.text: User settings outrank project settings for the model key; the developer should delete the model line from their user file and restart.
options.why: Project settings take precedence over user settings, so the user file is not what overrides the pin.

options.text: The developer's saved /model choice outranks the project file; they should run /model again to reset it.
options.why: /model writes the user settings file, which the project file outranks on the next launch.

explanation: Environment variables are not a level in the settings stack: ANTHROPIC_MODEL exported in the shell applies over the model key from any settings file. Diagnose model surprises by checking the launch environment first, and fix them there rather than by editing shared configuration.
reference: Claude Code docs — Model configuration; Claude Code docs — Settings files and precedence

stem: A team's dev environment uses a small model and a draft prompt, staging runs the production model with the candidate prompt, and production runs a pinned model with prompt v12. A developer notices the three also load different plugin sets and proposes making all environments identical to end the "it worked in staging" surprises. What is the better approach?

options.text: Make all three environments identical, including running the production model and prompt v12 in dev, so nothing can differ between them.
options.why: The differences are deliberate (cost in dev, candidate testing in staging); removing them does not make the remaining differences visible.

options.text: Keep the deliberate differences but declare each environment's model, prompt version and plugin versions in tracked config, promoted by review.
options.why: Environments differ on purpose; the fix is to make every difference declared and reviewable so a surprise can be traced to a specific declared value.

options.text: Unpin the model in every environment so all three always run the latest version.
options.why: Removes a declared variable and lets behaviour change with no commit, which makes surprises less attributable.

options.text: Move the environment configuration into the application code so it ships with each release.
options.why: Forces a release for every settings change and still leaves plugin versions undeclared.

explanation: Configuration management does not require identical environments; it requires that every difference be declared in tracked configuration (model, prompt version, plugin versions) so that behaviour can be attributed and promotion between environments is a reviewed change.
reference: Claude Code docs — Model configuration; Claude Code docs — Plugin dependencies

stem: A team inherits a Claude-based ticket classifier. Its prompts were edited in place in a dashboard, the model is referenced by a moving alias, and the eval set dates from launch a year ago while the ticket mix has changed. Leadership wants quality "improved." Which steps should come first? (Choose three.)

options.text: Pin the model to the specific ID currently being served.
options.why: Removes one undeclared variable so that any change in behaviour from now on can be attributed.

options.text: Capture the current prompt text as a versioned baseline in git.
options.why: Gives the running system a named version that evals can score and rollbacks can target.

options.text: Rebuild the eval set from a labeled sample of recent tickets and score the current system on it.
options.why: Restores a baseline that matches production traffic; without it no improvement can be measured.

options.text: Upgrade to the newest model immediately, since quality is the goal.
options.why: An improvement attempted before a baseline exists; nothing can show whether it helped.

options.text: Rewrite the prompts from scratch using current best practices.
options.why: Discards what the feature learned and changes behaviour with nothing to compare against.

options.text: Delete the stale eval set so it cannot mislead anyone.
options.why: Leaves less than before; the old set still documents the launch requirements until a replacement exists.

explanation: On an untracked system, restore measurability before improving anything: pin the inputs (model ID), give the prompt as it stands a version, and rebuild the evaluation set from recent traffic. Upgrading, rewriting or deleting first removes the ability to attribute the result.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations; Claude API docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A shared "summarize customer note" prompt is consumed by three applications: sales, support and billing. The owning team improves it for the sales app, and the sales staging run looks good. What should the team do before promoting the new version?

options.text: Schedule a maintenance window and roll the new version out behind a canary.
options.why: Staging the rollout limits blast radius but replaces assessment with observation of live users.

options.text: Announce the change in the shared channel with a summary of what improved, then promote it, since the sales staging run passed.
options.why: Communication is not assessment; the other two consumers' behaviour under the new version is still unknown.

options.text: Run each consuming application's own evals against the new version and coordinate the rollout on those results.
options.why: A shared prompt carries three sets of expectations; only per-consumer evaluation generates information about what the change does to each.

options.text: Promote it to all three applications at once, since a single prompt should have a single version.
options.why: Ships an unassessed change to two consumers that never tested it.

explanation: Prompt versioning with multiple consumers requires assessing the effect on each consumer before promotion. Announcing, scheduling or canarying are competent handling of a change whose effect has already been established; they do not establish it.
reference: Claude API docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations; Claude API docs — Prompt engineering overview

stem:
A repository's committed .claude/settings.json contains:

```json
{"permissions":{"allow":["Bash(npm test *)"],"deny":["Read(./.env)"]},
 "extraKnownMarketplaces":{"internal":{"source":{"source":"github","repo":"acme/claude-plugins"}}},
 "enabledPlugins":{"lint-kit@internal":true}}
```

A new hire clones the repository and starts an interactive session. Reading .env is blocked as expected, but Claude is still prompted before `npm test` and lint-kit is not installed. Colleagues on the same commit see neither problem. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The new hire has not accepted the workspace trust dialog for the folder, which gates the keys that grant capability while deny rules apply regardless.
options.why: Project allow rules and marketplace registration grant capability, so Claude Code holds them until the folder is trusted; deny rules only restrict and apply immediately, which matches the symptom exactly.

options.text: Project settings are read only when the user file sets the same keys, so the allow rule and marketplace must be duplicated in ~/.claude/settings.json.
options.why: Project settings are read on their own and merged with user settings; nothing needs to be duplicated.

options.text: Deny rules are evaluated first and, once one matches in a session, allow rules are skipped for the rest of it.
options.why: Deny-first ordering is applied per tool call; a deny on .env has no effect on an npm command.

options.text: Permission and plugin keys are honored only from .claude/settings.local.json, which is gitignored and so missing from the clone.
options.why: The local file is personal; the committed project file is precisely where shared allow rules and team plugins belong.

explanation: Repository-supplied configuration that grants capability, such as project allow rules, additional directories and marketplace registrations, takes effect only after the developer accepts the workspace trust dialog; keys that only restrict, such as deny rules, apply at once. A clone where deny works but allow and plugins do not is the signature of an untrusted folder.
reference: Claude Code docs — Configure permissions (project allow rules and workspace trust); Claude Code docs — Settings files and precedence

stem: Two internal plugins depend on the shared plugin secrets-vault: deploy-kit declares the range "^2.0" and audit-kit declares ">=2.3". Claude Code installs a shared dependency at the highest release tag that satisfies every installed plugin's range and refuses an install whose ranges cannot all be met. The audit team needs a feature that ships only in secrets-vault 3.1.0. What should the audit-kit maintainer do?

options.text: Change audit-kit's constraint to "^3.1" and publish, so users receive 3.1.0 on their next update.
options.why: ^2.0 and ^3.1 share no version, so anyone who has deploy-kit installed can no longer install the new audit-kit.

options.text: Have deploy-kit tested against 3.x and its range widened first, then move audit-kit's constraint to "^3.1".
options.why: The shared dependency moves only when every consumer's range admits the new major; widening the blocking constraint after testing is the reviewed path, and the tightened audit-kit range then resolves cleanly.

options.text: Drop the version constraint from audit-kit so it tracks the marketplace's latest tag.
options.why: deploy-kit's ^2.0 still holds the shared install on 2.x, and audit-kit would load against whatever version happens to be present.

options.text: Pin audit-kit to "=3.1.0" so that exact version is installed whatever other plugins declare.
options.why: An exact pin is still a range that ^2.0 cannot satisfy, so the conflict is the same.

explanation: A shared dependency can only move to a new major version when every consumer's range admits it. The maintainer who needs the upgrade coordinates with the plugin whose constraint blocks it: test that plugin against the new major, widen its range in a reviewed change, and only then tighten the dependent plugin's own constraint.
reference: Claude Code docs — Plugin dependencies

stem: A security team must ensure that (1) every engineer runs the vetted compliance-hooks plugin from the internal marketplace and cannot disable it, (2) engineers may install other plugins only from that internal marketplace or the official one, and (3) individual repositories can still auto-enable their own team plugins from the internal marketplace. Which configuration meets all three? (Choose two.)

options.text: In managed settings, allowlist the internal and official marketplaces with strictKnownMarketplaces and force compliance-hooks@internal on through enabledPlugins.
options.why: Managed settings cannot be overridden: the allowlist gates what users may add, and a managed enabledPlugins entry keeps the vetted plugin on for everyone.

options.text: Add a line to every CLAUDE.md instructing engineers to install compliance-hooks.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance for Claude, not a control on what plugins a person installs or disables.

options.text: In each repository's committed .claude/settings.json, register the internal marketplace with extraKnownMarketplaces and list the team's plugins in enabledPlugins.
options.why: Project settings travel with the clone and enable team plugins for everyone who trusts the folder, while staying within the managed allowlist.

options.text: Put compliance-hooks in every repository's .claude/settings.local.json.
options.why: The local file is gitignored and personal, so it reaches nobody else and can be edited away.

options.text: In managed settings, list every known third-party marketplace under blockedMarketplaces.
options.why: A blocklist can never enumerate every source engineers might add; the requirement is an allowlist.

explanation: Match each requirement to the scope with the right reach: organization-wide, non-overridable rules (marketplace allowlist, force-enabled plugins) go in managed settings, and team-level plugin enablement goes in the repository's committed project settings. Guidance files and personal local files cannot satisfy either.
reference: Claude Code docs — Manage Claude Code plugins for your organization; Claude Code docs — All settings (strictKnownMarketplaces, enabledPlugins)

stem:
A Claude Code-driven ticket-triage job started producing worse labels on Tuesday. No commit has landed in its repository since the previous Thursday. Its configuration reads:

```yaml
model: sonnet                       # family alias
prompt: s3://prompts/triage/latest.txt
plugins:
  - name: ticket-tools              # no version constraint
```

Which change to this configuration prevents this class of unattributable regression?

options.text: Upgrade the model to the newest release and re-run the job on Tuesday's tickets to see whether label quality recovers on its own.
options.why: Adds another unrecorded change; if quality moves, nobody can say which of four variables did it.

options.text: Replace each moving reference with a pinned one: a specific model ID, an immutable prompt version, and a plugin version range.
options.why: All three references can change with no commit; pinning them makes every future change a reviewed diff and gives a rollback a destination.

options.text: Remove the ticket-tools plugin, since an unconstrained dependency is the most likely culprit.
options.why: Removes a control to silence a symptom, without evidence, and leaves the alias and the latest prompt pointer free to move.

options.text: Roll the repository back to Thursday's commit and redeploy.
options.why: Nothing in the repository changed; the regression came from references that resolve outside it.

explanation: An unattributable regression means something changed that the repository does not record. A family alias, a prompt fetched from a latest pointer, and an unconstrained plugin dependency are each undeclared variables. Configuration management replaces them with explicit, pinnable versions so a change is always a diff and a rollback always has a target.
reference: Claude Code docs — Model configuration (model aliases); Claude Code docs — Plugin dependencies
